\nSharp (#) means raise the pitch of a n.en_GB:
Sharp (#) means raise the pitch of a note by a semitone, while flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone. Up means moving to the right on your piano keyboard while down means moving to the left. 

Here's an easy way to remember their difference: If you sit on something sharp, you would jump up. If you get a flat tyre on your car, it goes down.
\nSharp (#) means raise the pitch of a n.en_US:
Sharp (#) means raise the pitch of a note by a half step, while flat (♭) lowers it by a half step. Up means moving to the right on your piano keyboard while down means moving to the left. 

Here's an easy way to remember their difference: If you sit on something sharp, you would jump up. If you get a flat tire on your car, it goes down.

A scale is collection of notes within.en_GB:
A scale is a collection of notes within an octave that work together to evoke a certain emotional response.

There are several types of scales. However, the 2 most common types are the major scale and the minor scale. You can build both major and minor scales from any note.

The major scale is commonly associated with a happy or joyful sentiment, whereas the minor scale is known for evoking a sad or melancholic emotion.

Music encompasses a wide array of scales.en_GB:
Music encompasses a wide array of scales, and their usage frequencies can differ across regions, cultures, and musical genres.

One way to classify scales is by the number of notes they contain. In modern Western music, the 7-note scales, also known as heptatonic scales, dominate the scene. Among these, a particular subset called 'diatonic scales' or 'modes' holds significant importance. These 7 scales are all types of diatonic scales which means they have 7 notes and 2 intervals that are semitones, and 5 intervals that are tones.

To build minor chords, we stack a series.en_GB:
To build minor chords, we stack a series of thirds based on the minor scale starting from the root note. Here, we utilise the Aeolian or Natural Minor scale in the key of C as an example.

In this example the keyboard below displays the notes of the Aeolian scale as lettered yellow circles, with the root note highlighted in green. In major keys, the sharp 11th is often used to produce a richer, more harmonious sound.

Chord notes are built by stacking 3rds on top of a scale.

Using the 'W – W – H – W – W – W – H' pa.en_GB:
Using the 'T – T – S – T – T – T – S' pattern with the C major scale, you can see how the scale is built:
C - D - E - F - G - A - B.

For the A major scale, for example, you begin with the A. Then use the same pattern as above to get the following notes:
A - B - C# - D - E - F# - G#.

The 1st and the 8th notes have the same name here because they’re the exact same note — at the 8th note, the scale repeats itself.
